original_question: Consider a Hamiltonian system whose linearized operator, for example -Delta_f + v, has pure point spectrum, with part of that pure point spectrum dense in some finite interval. If the nonlinear part of the Hamiltonian is not short range, as in Hamiltonian partial differential equations posed on the whole space, do KAM tori still exist for that system?
target_in_paper: Section 2, Problem 2.8: the open problem asking whether KAM tori still exist for an infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian system when the linearized operator (for example, Ω^2 = -Δ_f + v) has pure point spectrum with a component dense in a finite interval, but the nonlinear part is no longer short range.
correct_elements: Your draft captures the core of the paper-faithful target very well: it uses the same model example of the linearized operator (-Δ_f + v), keeps the crucial pure-point-spectral hypothesis together with density in a finite interval, and asks exactly the right existence question about KAM tori after removing the short-range assumption. Those are the defining ingredients of Problem 2.8.
missing_details: The paper places this question in Section 2, whose topic is finite-dimensional KAM tori (quasi-periodic breathers) for infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian lattice systems, not a general survey question about all Hamiltonian PDEs on the whole space.
The question arises specifically after Theorem 2.5 and Theorem 2.6, which prove existence of such tori under short-range assumptions; that nearby positive result is part of the intended scope.

The paper's notion of short range is not merely informal: in the abstract Hamiltonian setting it is encoded by the interaction hypotheses (A2) and especially the exponential decay condition (2.14), while in the concrete discrete wave and discrete nonlinear Schrödinger examples it appears as the assumption that U and V are short range.

To stay fully faithful to the paper, the object sought should be described more precisely as KAM tori in the Section 2 sense, i.e. finite-dimensional invariant tori / quasi-periodic breathers inside an infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian system.
The paper does not formulate this as a PDE-only problem; the phrase 'as in Hamiltonian PDEs posed on the whole space' broadens the official formulation beyond the stated open problem.

The spectrum hypothesis in the paper is phrased as: the linearized operator is of pure point spectrum, and part of that spectrum is dense in some finite interval; it is worth keeping both parts explicitly.

The operator example is not arbitrary notation: it comes from the lattice linearization Ω^2 = -Δ_f + v introduced earlier from the discrete wave equation, so the refined question should preserve that concrete provenance if possible.
refined_question: In the Section 2 setting of finite-dimensional KAM tori (quasi-periodic breathers) for infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian lattice systems, suppose the linearized operator of the system—for example the lattice operator Ω^2 = -Δ_f + v—has pure point spectrum, with part of that spectrum dense in some finite interval. If one removes the short-range hypothesis on the nonlinear interaction (namely, the short-range assumptions used in Theorems 2.5 and 2.6, such as exponential spatial decay of the interaction or short-range U, V in the concrete lattice models), does the system still admit any KAM tori?
justification: This is Problem 2.8 rather than any statement from Section 1 or the neighboring Problem 2.9. The decisive match is the combination of two features: pure point spectrum with a dense component in a finite interval, and removal of the short-range nonlinearity assumption. Theorem 2.5 and Theorem 2.6 immediately set up the positive short-range case, including the possibility that the normal frequencies are dense in a finite interval; Remark 2.7 then explains why pure point spectrum is central and why continuous spectrum is a different issue; Problem 2.8 asks exactly the next question obtained by dropping short range while keeping the pure-point setting. Your mention of Hamiltonian PDEs on the whole space is an understandable analogy, but it is broader than the paper's official formulation, since Section 2 explicitly says it is focusing on short-range Hamiltonians rather than PDEs.
